title: Chord diagrams: audit directed flows before drawing ribbons
summary: Turn a directed source-to-destination matrix into an auditable chord layout without hiding self-flows or double-counting totals.
body:
Turn a directed source-to-destination matrix into an auditable chord layout without hiding self-flows or double-counting totals.

Fix the unit and direction first

A chord diagram curls a square flow matrix around a circle. One row identifies the source; one column identifies the destination. A matrix entry can represent parcels moved between depots, but it cannot mix parcel count with shipment value. Decide whether the story is directed before any ribbons are drawn: a transfer from North to East is not the same record as East to North. If the values describe mutual relationships rather than movements, use an undirected contract and explain how two mirrored cells are consolidated. Network graphs emphasize topology; chords emphasize the volume between a manageable set of named groups. Their apparent symmetry can mislead readers when source and destination have different meanings, so label the ends or use a visible directional cue.

Reconcile sectors and ribbons

For a directed matrix, the outbound total of a group is its row sum and inbound total is its column sum. Decide whether each sector encodes outbound alone or inbound plus outbound; otherwise a sector width may appear to contradict its label. The worked contract below reports both. A transfer from a group to itself belongs on the diagonal and must be kept or explicitly excluded. Draw a self-loop distinctly because it can consume a large share of an arc without crossing the center. A ribbon should have an auditable value in an accompanying table. Sankey diagrams are often clearer when a process has ordered stages and conservation across them must be inspected.

Keep categories and filters stable

Arc order changes which ribbons overlap and can make the same data look dense or sparse. Set one documented category order across periods and filtered views. If an unseen group is grouped into Other, publish which group IDs it contains and keep its membership fixed when comparing periods. An interaction should reveal source, destination, amount, unit, time window and whether the value is a self-loop. It should also disclose the current filter cohort. Linked filter state is part of the reading contract: a selected destination must not silently redefine the total behind each sector. Export the full matrix rather than only the visible top ribbons.

Use density as a stopping rule

With 47 groups, there can be 2,209 directed cells before any filtering. Even a complete and accurate chord can become an unreadable knot. Start with a ranked table, a small set of stable groups or a matrix heatmap when precise cell comparisons matter. Heatmaps preserve a fixed row-column grid and make absent flows easier to spot. If the chord is retained, annotate whether zeros mean no observed movement or unavailable data, and provide text alternatives for keyboard and screen-reader access. Test the display at narrow widths; hiding labels does not remove the underlying ambiguity.

Worked contract

def directed_flow_ledger(groups: list[str],
                         flows: dict[tuple[str, str], int]):
    if not groups or len(groups) != len(set(groups)) or any(not name for name in groups):
        raise ValueError("group names must be unique and nonempty")
    known = set(groups)
    if any(source not in known or target not in known or
           type(amount) is not int or amount < 0
           for (source, target), amount in flows.items()):
        raise ValueError("flow endpoints and amounts must be valid")
    matrix = [[flows.get((source, target), 0) for target in groups]
              for source in groups]
    outbound = {source: sum(matrix[index])
                for index, source in enumerate(groups)}
    inbound = {target: sum(matrix[index][column]
                           for index in range(len(groups)))
               for column, target in enumerate(groups)}
    assert sum(outbound.values()) == sum(inbound.values())
    return matrix, outbound, inbound

depots = ["North", "East", "West"]
transfers = {("North", "East"): 47, ("East", "North"): 13,
             ("North", "North"): 5, ("West", "East"): 29}
matrix, outbound, inbound = directed_flow_ledger(depots, transfers)
assert matrix[0] == [5, 47, 0]
assert outbound["North"] == 52
assert inbound["East"] == 76
assert sum(outbound.values()) == 94

Performance and operating cost

For G groups, matrix construction takes O(G²) time and O(G²) space even when most flows are zero. The sparse input map is better for storage and for very large networks; the dense matrix is useful only when the chosen renderer requires it. The ledger counts each directed transfer once, including a self-loop, and proves that aggregate outbound equals aggregate inbound. It does not turn the chart into a conservation model across time: inventory changes and external entries still require their own rows.

Common Mistakes

  • Adding both directions into one ribbon while calling the result directed.
  • Dropping self-loops because they do not cross the circle.
  • Changing arc order or the membership of Other between comparison panels.
  • Treating an unavailable matrix cell as an observed zero.

Validation drill

Audit 59 transfer routes between five depots. Reconcile each outbound and inbound subtotal, then compare a chord with a matrix table at phone width.

title: Bivariate choropleths: map two rates with a readable joint legend
summary: Classify two regional rates independently, then document all nine combinations, denominators and missing regions.
body:
Classify two regional rates independently, then document all nine combinations, denominators and missing regions.

Make each variable a comparable regional rate

A bivariate choropleth gives each area one color based on two measurements. First establish a meaningful rate for each variable, with its own numerator, denominator, period and units. Coloring counties by raw counts mainly maps population size, while comparing a rate from 2024 with another from 2026 can imply a joint pattern that never existed at one time. Check whether the geography is identical for both data sets and whether boundary changes have been resolved. Single-variable choropleths explain why boundary version and denominator belong in the legend. If two measures cannot be made comparable, separate maps with explicit units are the honest choice.

Classify each axis before mixing color

A typical joint legend has three classes for the horizontal measure and three for the vertical measure. That yields nine named combinations, such as low–high, not nine unlabeled shades. Declare two cut points per variable and how exact boundary values are handled. The code uses lower-inclusive classes: a value equal to the first cut moves into the middle class. Choose cut points against the analytic question, then freeze them across panels. Recomputing quantiles on every filter action can cause a region's color to change even when its rate does not. Shared scales apply to map panels too. A 3×3 legend should label both axes, their directions and the numeric boundaries.

Separate missingness from low values

A region missing either measure has no joint class. Give it a separate visible symbol and a table row explaining which measure is missing. A zero is a valid numeric value only when the upstream measurement process really observed zero. Suppression of small counts is not zero, and imputing it can distort a rate. Heatmap missing cells face the same distinction. Reconcile the number of mapped, missing, suppressed and excluded regions before styling. If an area has a tiny denominator, attach count and uncertainty in a companion table so its saturated color is not mistaken for strong evidence.

Use the map for patterns, the table for values

Nine colors are hard to decode from memory, especially when several patches are similar or the map is viewed on a small display. Test the palette under common color-vision differences and in grayscale; provide class text and both exact rates on focus or in a linked table. A bivariate map can suggest a spatial association, but it does not establish that one measure causes the other. Large regions occupy more screen area regardless of population, and neighboring regions are not independent evidence by default. Accessible color and text alternatives should be part of the export, not an afterthought. Include the breakpoints, data period, geographic key and unmapped-count summary with every image.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def joint_rate_classes(regions: list[tuple[str, float | None, float | None]],
                       first_cuts: tuple[float, float],
                       second_cuts: tuple[float, float]):
    if not (first_cuts[0] < first_cuts[1] and second_cuts[0] < second_cuts[1]):
        raise ValueError("each pair of cuts must increase")
    if len({region for region, _, _ in regions}) != len(regions):
        raise ValueError("region keys must be unique")
    cells = []
    for region, first_rate, second_rate in regions:
        if not region:
            raise ValueError("region key is required")
        if first_rate is None or second_rate is None:
            cells.append((region, None, first_rate, second_rate))
            continue
        if not isfinite(first_rate) or not isfinite(second_rate):
            raise ValueError("rates must be finite")
        first_class = sum(first_rate >= cut for cut in first_cuts)
        second_class = sum(second_rate >= cut for cut in second_cuts)
        cells.append((region, (first_class, second_class),
                      first_rate, second_rate))
    return cells

service_regions = [("ward-47", 12.0, 31.0),
                   ("ward-59", 19.0, 45.0),
                   ("ward-83", None, 24.0)]
classified = joint_rate_classes(service_regions, (12.0, 18.0), (25.0, 40.0))
assert classified[0][1] == (1, 1)
assert classified[1][1] == (2, 2)
assert classified[2][1] is None

Performance and operating cost

Classifying R regions takes O(R) time and O(R) output space; the nine-color lookup is constant size. The function preserves exact rates and missingness alongside class coordinates, and its assertions pin the breakpoint tie rule. It assumes both inputs are already compatible rates. Validate numerators, denominators, units, boundary version and time window upstream before interpreting any mapped class.

Common Mistakes

  • Mixing raw counts with rates in one joint legend.
  • Recomputing class breaks separately for each period while comparing colors.
  • Coloring a suppressed or absent rate as low.
  • Shipping nine colors without numeric boundaries or an accessible table.

Validation drill

Classify 47 wards for two service rates. Report all nine cell counts plus missing regions, and test whether the map stays interpretable in grayscale.

title: Dendrograms: read merge height without overreading leaf order
summary: Audit distance, linkage and cut height before labeling clusters from a hierarchical tree.
body:
Audit distance, linkage and cut height before labeling clusters from a hierarchical tree.

A tree is built from a distance rule

A dendrogram shows a sequence of cluster merges. Its shape depends first on what distance means: Euclidean distance on raw fields lets large-unit features dominate, while a domain-specific distance may weight errors or missingness differently. Standardize only when that operation fits the question and record the fitted scaling parameters. Then choose a linkage rule. Single linkage merges by the nearest pair of members and can chain points; complete linkage uses the farthest pair; average linkage uses the mean of pair distances. These are different cluster definitions, not styling options. Correlation heatmaps often sit next to a dendrogram, but the correlation-to-distance transformation must be stated if it creates the tree.

Read height, not horizontal spacing

The vertical coordinate of a merge records the linkage distance at which its child clusters join. Horizontal leaf placement is usually a layout choice: sibling branches can be rotated without changing any membership or merge distance. Do not infer that two neighboring leaf labels are the closest original pair merely because they appear adjacent. Put the distance metric and linkage rule in the caption, and label the merge-height axis with units or a dimensionless scale. A flat cut at a chosen height partitions the leaves, but that height is a decision threshold, not a statistical test. The chart question should say whether the reader needs a hierarchy, a fixed number of groups or actual pairwise distances.

Inspect unstable merges

Small changes in records or scaling can reorder merges near the same height. A visually dramatic split is not automatic evidence of a natural population boundary. Refit after reasonable perturbations, compare membership and report how often groups persist; keep the data snapshot fixed while changing one assumption at a time. If a leaf represents a collapsed branch, show how many original members it contains. Truncating a large dendrogram can hide lower merges, so label contracted nodes explicitly. Uncertainty displays are useful when the tree is used to support a decision, especially with few observations or noisy distances. Keep an accessible membership table for every cut shown.

Choose the right comparison view

A tree can hold many leaves but becomes difficult to read at phone width. For a few entities, a labeled distance matrix may answer the exact-pair question faster. For many groups, a cut-level summary and downloadable membership table are more useful than microscopic text. In linked views, selecting a branch should highlight its exact IDs in the associated chart without recomputing the clustering under the cursor. Linked filters should disclose whether they merely highlight a fixed tree or rebuild it from a filtered population. Rebuilding changes the merge history and needs a new analysis version in the export.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def average_linkage_merges(values: dict[str, float]):
    if len(values) < 2 or any(not label or not isfinite(value)
                              for label, value in values.items()):
        raise ValueError("at least two finite labeled observations are required")
    clusters = {label: (label,) for label in values}
    merges = []
    while len(clusters) > 1:
        candidates = []
        labels = sorted(clusters)
        for left_index, left in enumerate(labels):
            for right in labels[left_index + 1:]:
                distances = [abs(values[first] - values[second])
                             for first in clusters[left] for second in clusters[right]]
                candidates.append((sum(distances) / len(distances), left, right))
        height, left, right = min(candidates)
        members = tuple(sorted(clusters.pop(left) + clusters.pop(right)))
        cluster_id = "|".join(members)
        clusters[cluster_id] = members
        merges.append((members, height))
    return merges

sensor_offsets = {"sensor-47": 4.0, "sensor-59": 5.0,
                  "sensor-83": 19.0, "sensor-97": 21.0}
merges = average_linkage_merges(sensor_offsets)
assert merges[0] == (("sensor-47", "sensor-59"), 1.0)
assert merges[1] == (("sensor-83", "sensor-97"), 2.0)
assert merges[2][1] == 15.5

Performance and operating cost

This transparent teaching implementation recomputes all candidate average distances at every merge. For N observations it uses O(N³) time in the worst case and O(N²) temporary space: each merge compares pair distances across the current partition; use a tested clustering library for real data. Its scalar absolute-distance rule is deliberately narrow. The output provides memberships and heights, not leaf x-coordinates. Those can be rearranged without changing the hierarchy.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading adjacent leaves as the closest original observations.
  • Changing the distance metric or scaling without documenting a new tree.
  • Treating a chosen cut height as a significance threshold.
  • Truncating branches without their member counts or a membership table.

Validation drill

Cluster 47 sensor offsets using two distance definitions. Save both trees, compare cut memberships and explain which merges changed because of the metric.

title: Probability calibration plots: compare predicted risk with observed frequency
summary: Build a reliability table with honest bin counts, event rates and a fixed evaluation cohort.
body:
Build a reliability table with honest bin counts, event rates and a fixed evaluation cohort.

Separate ranking from calibrated probability

A score can rank likely events well yet overstate their chance. A calibration plot asks whether cases assigned a given probability experience the event at approximately that frequency. For an equipment-alert model, a group with average predicted failure probability 0.31 should have an observed failure share near 0.31 over a sufficiently large, representative evaluation set. This is not a claim about any single device. Regression overlays often invite a best-fit line; a calibration plot instead compares observed and predicted rates against the identity diagonal. Ranking metrics, decision thresholds and the cost of false alarms answer different questions and should be displayed separately.

Construct bins without concealing support

Partition predictions with a stated rule. Equal-width bins have stable numeric boundaries but may leave some bins thin; equal-count bins balance support yet their boundaries move between cohorts. For each nonempty bin, plot mean predicted probability on x and observed event fraction on y. Include count and event count in a table or label, because a point based on 7 cases is not as stable as one based on 700. Do not join empty bins with a line. The code uses fixed equal-width bins and makes p=1 belong to the final bin. Small-sample displays explain why approximate agreement needs interval context, especially near the extremes.

Protect the evaluation split

Calibration estimated on the same records used to fit or tune a model is optimistic. Hold out an evaluation period or cohort and keep its definition stable. If scores are recalibrated, fit that transformation on a separate calibration set, then evaluate it on untouched data. Log model version, score timestamp, outcome window and censoring or delayed-label policy. A device marked as no failure before its observation window closes is not a verified negative. Provisional periods must be separated from complete labels. Also show prevalence: when base failure rate shifts between cohorts, the curve may move even if the model's ranking stays useful.

Inspect slices and drift carefully

A global curve can hide one badly miscalibrated plant or device family. Compare slices only when each has enough cases, and keep the same bin boundaries and evaluation window. Report omitted records and missing scores. Point movement between months may be sampling noise, model drift or a change in who gets scored; the plot alone cannot distinguish them. Small multiples with shared scales make comparisons less deceptive, while an export manifest keeps model and data versions attached to the image. Provide the underlying bin table so readers can check the plotted rates rather than measuring the diagonal by eye.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def calibration_bins(records: list[tuple[str, float, bool]], width: int = 5):
    if type(width) is not int or width <= 0:
        raise ValueError("bin count must be positive")
    identifiers = [device_id for device_id, _, _ in records]
    if len(identifiers) != len(set(identifiers)) or any(not item for item in identifiers):
        raise ValueError("device IDs must be unique and nonempty")
    bins = [[0, 0.0, 0] for _ in range(width)]
    for _, probability, failed in records:
        if (not isfinite(probability) or not 0 <= probability <= 1
                or type(failed) is not bool):
            raise ValueError("probabilities and event flags must be valid")
        bucket = min(int(probability * width), width - 1)
        bins[bucket][0] += 1
        bins[bucket][1] += probability
        bins[bucket][2] += failed
    return [(bucket, count, score_sum / count, events / count, events)
            for bucket, (count, score_sum, events) in enumerate(bins)
            if count]

inspection_results = [("unit-47", 0.22, False),
                      ("unit-59", 0.31, True),
                      ("unit-83", 0.37, False),
                      ("unit-97", 1.0, True)]
reliability = calibration_bins(inspection_results)
assert reliability[0] == (1, 3, 0.3, 1 / 3, 1)
assert reliability[1] == (4, 1, 1.0, 1.0, 1)

Performance and operating cost

For N predictions and B fixed bins, accumulation takes O(N + B) time and O(B + N) space because unique IDs are validated. Empty bins are omitted rather than invented. The four-record check demonstrates bin assignment and arithmetic, not credible calibration evidence; real evaluation needs sufficient support, a held-out cohort and uncertainty intervals. The function does not estimate those intervals or repair delayed labels.

Common Mistakes

  • Using training records as the final reliability evaluation.
  • Plotting one bin point without its case count or event count.
  • Calling a high-ranking score calibrated without comparing observed frequency.
  • Treating unfinished outcome windows as verified negatives.

Validation drill

Hold out 470 device predictions. Build fixed bins for two months, print counts and event rates, then identify whether a shifted curve also coincides with changed prevalence or incomplete labels.

body:

  • Horizon charts: trade vertical space for a harder value lookup
  • Animated charts: do not let motion invent data

Event and category evidence

  • Survival curves: show who remains at risk after each event

title: Data visualization
summary: Choose charts from the question, unit, denominator, and uncertainty the reader needs to judge.
body:
Choose charts from the question, unit, denominator, and uncertainty the reader needs to judge.

Where to begin

Start with the decision a reader must make. Then choose an encoding that preserves the relevant comparison, define the aggregation grain, and check scale, distribution, small samples, accessibility, and dashboard provenance. The linked project turns those choices into a reviewable operations display.

Choose the right method

A chart with many filters can become expensive to compute and hard to interpret. Pre-aggregate only at a grain that preserves the intended question, and state when a denominator or sample size changes under a filter.

title: Sankey diagrams: reconcile flows before sizing links
summary: Make every stage transition accountable, including dropouts and unobserved destinations.
body:
Make every stage transition accountable, including dropouts and unobserved destinations.

A link represents a transfer

A Sankey diagram uses link width to encode quantity moving between stages. The visual claim is stronger than a list of counts: a unit leaving one stage must either enter a named next stage, exit the process, or remain unobserved under a declared cutoff. If 81 claims enter triage and 47 reach review, the other 34 need a visible destination, not an unexplained gap. Unit-of-analysis rules prevent one claim with multiple events from becoming several flows.

Give nodes stage-specific identities

The same label at two stages does not necessarily describe the same state. Use stable stage and state IDs, deduplicate by entity and transition, and decide how repeated or backward transitions are handled. A diagram that assumes a directed acyclic process can fail when work returns to triage. In that case, either aggregate one chosen journey window or use another graph view that represents loops. Network diagrams can show cycles, though they answer a different question.

Check conservation at intermediate stages

For a closed interval, incoming and outgoing measured quantities at a transit state should balance after explicit additions, losses and stock change. If 47 enter review and 42 leave, five may still be in progress; add a pending exit or annotate the stock. For a live interval, arrivals and departures can differ because the cohort has not matured. Attach extraction time and observation horizon to the flow, and never compare incoming of one cohort to outgoing of another. Provisional periods need separate handling.

Make ordering and scale inspectable

Link crossing is partly a layout choice. Reordering nodes can reduce crossings without changing the data, so visual proximity must not be treated as a causal relation. Show quantities, units and denominators in text or a companion table. Fixed link colors can track origin across stages, but blending may obscure a small branch; direct labels or hover summaries help. Accessible alternatives should list source, target and value. Large graphs may be better as a transition table.

Worked contract

from collections import defaultdict

def reconcile_flow(
    links: list[tuple[str, str, int]], transit_nodes: set[str]
) -> dict[str, tuple[int, int]]:
    incoming = defaultdict(int)
    outgoing = defaultdict(int)
    for source, target, quantity in links:
        if not source or not target or quantity < 0:
            raise ValueError("invalid flow link")
        outgoing[source] += quantity
        incoming[target] += quantity
    balances = {node: (incoming[node], outgoing[node]) for node in transit_nodes}
    if any(entered != left for entered, left in balances.values()):
        raise ValueError(f"unreconciled transit node: {balances}")
    return balances

journey = [("intake", "review", 47),
           ("intake", "unobserved-exit", 34),
           ("review", "closed", 42),
           ("review", "pending", 5)]
assert reconcile_flow(journey, {"review"}) == {"review": (47, 47)}
assert sum(value for source, _, value in journey if source == "intake") == 81

Performance and operating cost

For E links and T transit nodes, accumulation and reconciliation take O(E + T) expected time and O(V) space for V encountered nodes. Layout can be substantially more expensive and depends on the rendering algorithm; do not mix that cost with the inexpensive accounting check. A real workflow also checks duplicate entity transitions and whether stock change belongs in the diagram. The example treats all links as counts in one cohort and one period.

Common Mistakes

  • Hiding exits to make the main path look complete.
  • Counting multiple events from one entity as separate stage transfers.
  • Balancing one period's arrivals against another period's departures.
  • Assuming node position or link crossing has business meaning.

Validation drill

Model 81 claims through intake, review and closure. Add a pending branch and an unobserved exit; fail the reconciliation when either is removed, then render a transition table beside the flow.

title: Network graphs: define nodes and edges before trusting the layout
summary: Check identity, direction, duplicates and degree before placing nodes on a canvas.
body:
Check identity, direction, duplicates and degree before placing nodes on a canvas.

The edge is the claim

A node-link graph represents entities and relationships. Before running a force layout, specify whether an edge means a message, a transaction, a dependency or a co-occurrence, and whether direction matters. Two messages from depot A to depot B may be two events or one weighted relationship. Resolve that choice at the declared grain. Stable node IDs prevent two accounts with the same display name from merging. The unit of analysis extends to graph edges.

Layout distance is not a metric

Force layouts position nodes by an algorithm balancing constraints. Nearby nodes may be strongly connected, but the distance is not automatically a business quantity; changing a random seed, viewport or graph subset can move them. Pin important positions or show a fixed comparison layout when inspecting versions. Report quantitative graph measures separately with their definitions. Comparison panels should preserve a stable node identity and comparable viewport.

Count what selection removes

A filtered network can make a high-degree node appear isolated if many of its neighbors are hidden. Show selected and total degree separately or state that the graph describes only the visible subgraph. Validate dangling edges whose endpoints are absent; do not let the renderer silently discard them. For large graphs, aggregate by a declared community or show a ranked adjacency table, because a dense hairball hides paths and edge direction. Resolution limits apply to edges and nodes as much as to points in a chart.

Design for inspection

Hover-only relationships are inaccessible on touch and keyboard. Provide a searchable node list, ordered neighbor table, edge direction labels and a way to inspect an entity without relying on color. Keep private identifiers out of public graph exports. A link of width 8 should name the weight unit and time interval; do not use width for one measure and tooltip for another. Text alternatives carry exact relationships that an overview cannot show.

Worked contract

from collections import defaultdict

def directed_degrees(
    node_ids: set[str], links: list[tuple[str, str, int]]
) -> dict[str, tuple[int, int]]:
    if not node_ids:
        raise ValueError("empty node set")
    incoming = defaultdict(int)
    outgoing = defaultdict(int)
    for source, target, weight in links:
        if source not in node_ids or target not in node_ids or weight <= 0:
            raise ValueError("dangling edge or nonpositive weight")
        outgoing[source] += weight
        incoming[target] += weight
    return {node: (incoming[node], outgoing[node]) for node in node_ids}

degrees = directed_degrees(
    {"depot-47", "depot-81", "depot-94"},
    [("depot-47", "depot-81", 31),
     ("depot-81", "depot-94", 8)])
assert degrees["depot-81"] == (31, 8)
assert sum(value[0] for value in degrees.values()) == 39

Performance and operating cost

For V nodes and E links, endpoint validation and weighted-degree counting take O(V + E) expected time and O(V) space. Layout may take many iterative passes and dominate CPU; this accounting step should run first so bad graph data does not get disguised by an attractive arrangement. The function sums weights and permits repeated directed pairs by design. If the chart promises one edge per pair, aggregate and count duplicates explicitly before layout.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating screen distance from a force layout as an exact relationship strength.
  • Discarding edges with missing endpoints without an audit count.
  • Mixing event count with unique-neighbor degree.
  • Comparing two filtered layouts without identifying removed nodes and edges.

Validation drill

Map handoffs among 31 service teams. Add a duplicate label, a dangling edge and a filtered-out hub; preserve stable IDs and report both visible and full-graph weighted degrees.

title: Choropleth maps: normalize counts and audit boundary coverage
summary: Join measures to the right polygons, use a stated denominator, and distinguish unmapped places from zero-valued regions.
body:
Join measures to the right polygons, use a stated denominator, and distinguish unmapped places from zero-valued regions.

Area color is not an event count

A choropleth fills geographic regions according to a measure. Large polygons occupy more pixels and can dominate attention even when they contain few people or events. Raw incident counts often track exposure, such as population or active deliveries, more than risk. For a comparable rate, carry numerator and denominator for each polygon and specify the period. Exposure-based rates explain why 8 incidents across 47,000 trips differ from 8 across 470 trips. A map can still show counts when workload is the question; label it as a count map.

Join by stable region identity

Names drift, abbreviations collide, and administrative boundaries change. Join facts to geometry with stable region IDs and a boundary version. Report unmatched fact IDs, polygons with no measure, duplicate assignments and overlapping boundaries before rendering. Spatial joins are a separate operation from coloring polygons; they can duplicate a record if geometries overlap. If one region splits midyear, a before-after map needs a common boundary basis or an explicit break. Do not let a chart library silently drop unmatched regions.

Projection and extent shape perception

A projection transforms coordinates into map space. It can distort area, shape or distance; no flat map preserves everything. For regional comparison, keep the same projection, extent and viewport across panels, and avoid interpreting the visible area of a polygon as its population. Insets for distant regions need clear labels and scale context. If exact comparison of rates matters more than location, provide a sorted bar chart alongside the map. Choose the visual that serves the question, not merely the available geometry.

Class breaks are an editorial decision

Equal-width bins, quantile bins and fixed policy thresholds answer different questions. A quantile palette can assign different colors to tiny numeric differences when many regions cluster tightly; fixed thresholds can leave some colors unused. Print numeric breakpoints and keep them stable when comparing dates. Use a separate treatment for missing data and low-exposure suppression. Color-domain rules carry over to map legends. Keep the original rate in the accessible table and tooltip; color bins are a summary, not the data.

Protect sensitive locations

Very small denominators can make rates unstable and expose information about a few people or facilities. Define a minimum publishable group size, aggregate or suppress as appropriate, and show a visible suppressed state. Do not infer that a blank region has zero risk. Location privacy and small-sample display belong to the same release review. Test a region with no geometry, a polygon with no observation, a zero numerator and a zero denominator separately.

Worked contract

def regional_rates(
    boundary_ids: set[str],
    incident_counts: dict[str, tuple[int, int]]
) -> dict[str, tuple[str, float | None]]:
    unknown = set(incident_counts) - boundary_ids
    if unknown:
        raise ValueError(f"facts without geometry: {sorted(unknown)}")
    result = {}
    for region_id in boundary_ids:
        if region_id not in incident_counts:
            result[region_id] = ("missing", None)
            continue
        incidents, trips = incident_counts[region_id]
        if not 0 <= incidents <= trips:
            raise ValueError("invalid regional counts")
        result[region_id] = ("no-exposure", None) if trips == 0 else (
            "observed", incidents / trips)
    return result

rates = regional_rates({"zone-47", "zone-81", "zone-94"},
                       {"zone-47": (8, 470), "zone-81": (0, 81)})
assert rates["zone-47"][1] == 8 / 470
assert rates["zone-81"] == ("observed", 0.0)
assert rates["zone-94"] == ("missing", None)

Performance and operating cost

For B boundary IDs and M measured regions, this join-and-rate check takes O(B + M) expected time and O(B) output space using hash sets. Rendering cost depends on polygon vertex count, projection and viewport clipping, none of which this code performs. Simplify geometry only to a documented tolerance and keep an exact source for hit tests. A cached tile or geometry file must carry the same boundary version as the measures. The code distinguishes zero and missing; a real publication layer also enforces suppression and uncertainty policy.

Common Mistakes

  • Coloring raw counts as if the map showed per-person or per-trip risk.
  • Joining on human-readable region names without checking unmatched and duplicated keys.
  • Treating a missing polygon or missing measure as zero.
  • Changing map bounds or class breaks between comparison dates.

Validation drill

Map 23 service zones with one split boundary, one missing measure and one zone below the publishable exposure threshold. Reconcile region IDs and rates before drawing polygons; add a sorted rate table for exact comparison.

title: Accessible charts: encode meaning without relying on color alone
summary: A chart needs legible labels, keyboard access where interactive, and a text route to the same substantive data.
body:
A chart needs legible labels, keyboard access where interactive, and a text route to the same substantive data.

Keep meaning redundant

A red and green pair is not enough to distinguish two completion series. Use direct labels, distinct line styles or marker shapes, and a legend that names the measured groups. Color can reinforce meaning but should not carry it alone. Axis labels must include units and remain legible at narrow widths.

Write a useful alternative

An image alternative should state the main comparison and notable exception, not simply “bar chart.” A companion table should expose exact values, periods and denominators for readers who cannot use the graphic. For an interactive chart, its filter controls need visible names, keyboard focus and a text update when the dataset changes.

Test the states

Check high zoom, narrow layout, monochrome output and keyboard-only interaction. A hover tooltip is not an adequate source of the only exact value. If a tooltip reports 74 percent but the accessible table says 73.6 percent, declare rounding once and use it consistently. Dashboard filters must update both representations together.

Budget complexity

A dense chart with 40 small labels may be technically accessible but still hard to scan. Reduce visible series, use a stable sort and provide a drill-down or table for detail. Retain disclosure of hidden groups and totals so simplification does not selectively remove an unfavorable channel.

Implementation

def chart_alt_text(period_label, channel_rates):
    measured = [(channel, rate) for channel, rate in channel_rates.items() if rate is not None]
    if not measured:
        return f"{period_label}: no channel has an eligible denominator."
    highest_channel, highest_rate = max(measured, key=lambda item: item[1])
    return (f"{period_label}: {len(measured)} channels measured; "
            f"{highest_channel} has the highest completion rate at {highest_rate:.1%}.")

Performance and operating cost

A short alternative over C channels costs O(C) time and O(C) temporary space in this implementation. For larger datasets, aggregate once and reuse the exact result for chart, table and alternative text to prevent divergence.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not rely on hue alone to identify a series.
  • Do not put the only exact value in a pointer-only tooltip.
  • Do not write alternative text from stale data after filters change.

title: Correlation heatmaps: show pairwise coverage before interpreting color
summary: Keep a correlation matrix honest about missing pairs, redundant cells and feature order.
body:
Keep a correlation matrix honest about missing pairs, redundant cells and feature order.

The matrix has more than coefficients

A correlation cell describes observations shared by two variables. With missing fields, one cell may use 810 records and another 47; identical color saturation hides that difference. Carry a second matrix of pairwise counts and expose it in labels, tooltips or a companion table. A blank pair means insufficient shared records or an undefined statistic, not zero association. Missing-cell rules distinguish these states. Record which rows passed eligibility filters before calculating either matrix.

Choose a missing-data contract

Pairwise deletion uses every available pair but can give each cell a different population. Complete-case deletion holds one population constant but may discard most records and change who remains. State the choice and counts. A constant column has zero variance and no Pearson correlation; mark it undefined. Do not fill its cell with zero merely to complete a square. Dataset grain and join checks should precede calculation so duplicated rows do not inflate confidence.

Order features for the reading task

Alphabetical order is stable and auditable. A domain order groups related measures. Data-driven clustering can reveal blocks, but the clustering method and input matrix become part of the result; changing order between periods makes comparison harder. Fix order for side-by-side charts, or record the exact order for each export. Show a legend centered on zero with identical limits in every panel. Scale integrity prevents a weak coefficient from receiving the same shade as a strong one elsewhere.

Do not infer a mechanism

A large coefficient can arise from shared time trends, repeated entities, selection or a third variable. The matrix is a screen for questions, not proof that changing one field changes another. Confirm striking cells with paired scatter plots, units and source counts; outliers can dominate a linear coefficient. Avoid painting both triangles when space is tight, since the duplicate area adds no information. Dense scatter views help inspect what the matrix compressed. Describe the population and time range beside every matrix.

Worked contract

from math import sqrt

def pearson_pair(records: list[dict[str, float | None]],
                 left: str, right: str) -> tuple[float | None, int]:
    pairs = [(record[left], record[right]) for record in records
             if record.get(left) is not None and record.get(right) is not None]
    count = len(pairs)
    if count < 2:
        return None, count
    left_mean = sum(value[0] for value in pairs) / count
    right_mean = sum(value[1] for value in pairs) / count
    cross = sum((x - left_mean) * (y - right_mean) for x, y in pairs)
    left_square = sum((x - left_mean) ** 2 for x, _ in pairs)
    right_square = sum((y - right_mean) ** 2 for _, y in pairs)
    if not left_square or not right_square:
        return None, count
    return cross / sqrt(left_square * right_square), count

shipments = [{"distance": 47, "cost": 81},
             {"distance": 59, "cost": 97},
             {"distance": 71, "cost": 113},
             {"distance": 83, "cost": None}]
coefficient, paired_count = pearson_pair(shipments, "distance", "cost")
assert round(coefficient, 12) == 1 and paired_count == 3

Performance and operating cost

For P fields and N rows, a direct full matrix performs O(P²N) pair work and stores O(P²) coefficients and counts. Columnar execution can lower constant costs, but pairwise coverage still needs explicit accounting. The example returns undefined for insufficient pairs or constant values and does not provide a significance test. A precise coefficient on three shared rows is weak evidence for a broad population claim.

Common Mistakes

  • Showing a coefficient without its pairwise record count.
  • Coloring undefined correlations as zero.
  • Changing row order across comparison periods without notice.
  • Treating a strong correlation as a causal intervention result.

Validation drill

Build a five-field matrix where one field appears in only 47 of 810 records. Show the count matrix beside the coefficient matrix, then compare pairwise and complete-case populations.

title: Chart design starts with a question, unit and visual encoding
summary: A chart is a visual comparison over defined observations; its marks and axes must preserve the quantity the reader is meant to compare.
body:
A chart is a visual comparison over defined observations; its marks and axes must preserve the quantity the reader is meant to compare.

Write the comparison

A receipt operations report might ask whether the share of reviews completed within 24 hours changed by channel. That is a rate by category and period, not a count of tickets. Record the population, numerator, denominator, time window and update cadence before picking a shape. Metric denominators belong in the chart contract because a change in eligibility can look like a change in performance.

Map quantities to marks

Position on a common scale is useful for comparing rates across channels; a bar chart makes zero a visible reference. Use a line only when adjacent points are connected by an ordered process such as time. A scatter plot asks whether two numeric quantities move together. A decorative shape must not imply a numerical relationship the dataset does not contain.

Preserve context

Show units, sample counts and the period cutoff. A rate can rise when a low-volume channel disappears even if no channel improves. Add a small companion table or labels with denominators when that composition matters. Aggregation grain determines what the visual mark actually represents. Never use a legend to hide a definition required to read the chart.

Specify a review fixture

Create one channel with 34 timely reviews out of 47 receipts and another with 18 out of 23. The second bar is higher despite its lower count. Ask a reviewer to state that distinction from the figure alone, then test an empty channel. Empty is missing evidence, not a zero percent service rate.

Implementation

def channel_completion_rate(timely_count, eligible_count):
    if eligible_count < 0 or timely_count < 0 or timely_count > eligible_count:
        raise ValueError("invalid receipt counts")
    return None if eligible_count == 0 else timely_count / eligible_count

channel_rates = {
    "portal": channel_completion_rate(34, 47),
    "email": channel_completion_rate(18, 23),
}

Performance and operating cost

Computing C channel rates is O(C) time and O(C) output space. Rendering cost grows with the number of marks, labels and interaction states; filter or aggregate only under a stated rule so the viewer can recover the denominator.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not substitute counts for rates when channel volumes differ.
  • Do not connect unordered categories with a line.
  • Do not render an empty denominator as a measured zero.

title: Uncertainty on charts: show denominators and intervals beside estimates
summary: A plotted estimate is not a population fact; its uncertainty and sample unit affect how strongly a visual difference can be read.
body:
A plotted estimate is not a population fact; its uncertainty and sample unit affect how strongly a visual difference can be read.

Show the independent count

Two channels can both report a 75 percent completion rate, yet one may have 12 receipts and another 12,000. Put eligible counts near marks or in an accessible companion table. If customers submit repeated receipts, the independent count may be customers rather than rows. Cluster resampling keeps those observations together.

Choose an interval contract

Specify the estimator, interval construction, confidence level and sampling unit. Error bars from an independent-row formula are misleading when assignments or outcomes cluster by reviewer. A confidence interval describes a repeated-sampling procedure; it is not a probability distribution over the displayed fixed rate. Coverage requires a valid observation process.

Separate overlap from decision

Overlapping intervals do not by themselves establish that a difference is absent, and nonoverlap is not a universal experiment test. If the task is to compare channels, calculate and display an interval for the difference under the study design. Pair this with practical limits: a two-point change may matter only above a declared volume or cost threshold.

Handle thin groups

A filter may leave one receipt or none. Use a visible “insufficient data” state rather than a narrow-looking point with absent error bars. Check that each interval is within the metric domain and that chart tooling does not clip it without notice. Keep the raw numerator and denominator available for audit.

Implementation

def interval_mark(point_rate, lower_rate, upper_rate, eligible_count):
    if eligible_count < 2:
        return {"state": "insufficient_data", "eligible_count": eligible_count}
    if not 0 <= lower_rate <= point_rate <= upper_rate <= 1:
        raise ValueError("invalid rate interval")
    return {"state": "measured", "point": point_rate,
            "lower": lower_rate, "upper": upper_rate, "eligible_count": eligible_count}

Performance and operating cost

Formatting M intervals is O(M) time and space. Interval estimation may be much more expensive, especially when resampling clusters; calculate it in a versioned data job and render the stored estimate with its construction metadata.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not draw error bars without naming their meaning.
  • Do not use receipt count as the independent sample size when customers repeat.
  • Do not interpret overlapping intervals as a complete test of a difference.

title: Small multiples: compare groups with honest scales and facet order
summary: Repeat one chart grammar across groups, then choose shared or local axes according to the intended comparison.
body:
Repeat one chart grammar across groups, then choose shared or local axes according to the intended comparison.

A facet is a repeated measurement frame

Small multiples split the same visual grammar into panels, one per group. They reduce line crossings and legend lookup when a single plot has too many series. The gain depends on consistency: each panel should use the same measure, time window, mark type and aggregation rule. A panel for customer tickets and a panel for revenue do not become comparable simply because they share a grid. Declare the measure before arranging panels. Keep a visible label on each panel; color alone is insufficient.

Shared scales answer magnitude questions

If the reader needs to know which depot has the largest delay, a shared y-domain lets equal heights mean equal values. Local y-domains can make a low-volume depot's variation legible, but a steep line then no longer means a larger absolute change. If independent domains are necessary, print the local minimum and maximum in every panel and avoid a headline about cross-panel magnitude. Axis integrity applies to every facet. For percentages, a fixed zero-to-one domain is often an honest baseline; for residuals around zero, a symmetric domain may expose sign and spread better.

Keep the time window and missingness aligned

Shared x-axes help readers distinguish a simultaneous event from a panel-specific shift. A region with no observations on Wednesday should show a gap, not compress its calendar so Thursday occupies Wednesday's position. When groups enter the system at different times, an aligned calendar makes the unequal exposure visible. Time-series gap rules should be applied before faceting. If panels use different time windows by design, label them prominently and avoid visual comparison of positions.

Order panels for the task

Alphabetical order is stable but often unhelpful when inspecting performance. Sorting by a predeclared baseline or current value can put high-risk groups first; automatic resorting on every hover makes the layout hard to track. Record the sort key and freeze it for an analysis session. Do not omit small groups without stating a threshold and the number omitted. Small-sample uncertainty often explains why an apparently extreme panel should receive inspection rather than a confident ranking.

Budget the screen

Thirty tiny panels may be technically complete yet unreadable on a phone. Allow searching or paging through stable groups while keeping the same scale contract. A summary panel can show the total or reference band, but it must follow the same population rules. Test keyboard order and screen-reader panel labels. If each facet needs a unique tooltip, interaction cost grows with the number of panels; prioritize a simple data table for exact values. A chart grid should make comparisons easier, not force the reader to memorize dozens of legends.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def facet_domains(series: dict[str, list[float]],
                  shared: bool) -> dict[str, tuple[float, float]]:
    if not series or any(not values for values in series.values()):
        raise ValueError("each facet needs observed values")
    if any(not isfinite(value) for values in series.values() for value in values):
        raise ValueError("non-finite plotted value")
    if shared:
        values = [value for group in series.values() for value in group]
        domain = (min(values), max(values))
        return {name: domain for name in series}
    return {name: (min(values), max(values)) for name, values in series.items()}

depot_delays = {"north": [18, 47], "south": [3, 8]}
assert facet_domains(depot_delays, True)["south"] == (3, 47)
assert facet_domains(depot_delays, False)["south"] == (3, 8)

Performance and operating cost

For N values across G groups, scanning domains takes O(N + G) time. The shared branch stores an extra O(N) flattened list for clarity; a streaming minimum and maximum reduce that auxiliary memory to O(1), while the returned G domains still need O(G) space. Rendering cost scales with both the number of panels and marks. A UI that rerenders every facet after each filter may become slow even when the domain calculation is cheap; memoize by the complete filter and data-version key only when measurements justify it.

Common Mistakes

  • Using independent y-domains while claiming one group has the larger magnitude.
  • Dropping missing dates and shifting one panel's x positions relative to the rest.
  • Reordering facets during interaction without labeling the sort key.
  • Suppressing tiny cohorts without reporting how many groups were hidden.

Validation drill

Facet five depot delay series on one weekly calendar. Produce a shared-scale view for absolute comparison and a labeled independent-scale view for within-depot variation; write down which conclusions differ.

title: Chart exports: carry the data, filters and render contract together
summary: Give exported images an auditable data table and a compact manifest of the choices that produced them.
body:
Give exported images an auditable data table and a compact manifest of the choices that produced them.

An image is not the full evidence

A PNG captures pixels; it does not preserve the records, filter predicates, missingness states or exact values behind them. SVG retains scalable geometry, but it can still omit the underlying analytical contract. For a decision-grade chart, export an image, a machine-readable table of plotted values and a manifest describing the query and rendering choices. The package should answer which source snapshot, cohort, units, time zone, grouping rule, axis domain, palette and code version produced the picture. Dashboard provenance supplies these ingredients; export binds them to an artifact.

Version the plotted data product

A chart may use raw events, daily aggregates or a reduced display level. The export must name that level. Include a dataset snapshot or immutable revision, plus the report's as-of time when corrections are possible. A hash of canonical manifest bytes detects accidental changes to the manifest; it does not authenticate a source by itself. If integrity across systems matters, sign the package through a trusted release path. Never include private identifiers or unmasked rows merely because a chart view was authorized. Data classification still governs exports.

Keep visible and downloadable values aligned

The CSV or JSON table must use the same filters, denominator, sort, unit and missing-value policy as the displayed chart. If the chart shows rounded percentages, include underlying counts and unrounded rates in the data export while documenting the display rounding. A tooltip, table and image title should agree on the period and finalization status. Linked filters can change the cohort moments before a user clicks export; capture one state and one data version atomically for the whole package.

Make the visual portable and accessible

An SVG is useful for vector editing and high-resolution print, but font substitution and external styles can change its appearance. A PNG is more predictable but loses scale and selectable text. Include an accessible text summary and data table in either case. Document the output size, color profile where relevant, and the scale tick labels. Text alternatives should describe the main pattern, notable exceptions and uncertainty rather than repeat a generic chart title. For a public download, test that no hidden private series remain in SVG markup or embedded metadata.

Recreate before release

Re-run the export from its manifest in a clean environment. Compare plotted counts, axis limits, filters, title, source generation and checksum, allowing only declared rendering differences such as font rasterization. A changed query definition should make an old package non-reproducible by design; report that conflict instead of silently rendering with today's code. Keep an editorial preview for review, then publish an immutable artifact reference when the chart is used in a report or audit. Reduced series need the level and bucket rule in the manifest.

Worked contract

import hashlib
import json

def chart_manifest(query_id: str, dataset_version: str,
                   filters: dict[str, list[str]],
                   axis_domain: tuple[float, float],
                   plotted_rows: int) -> tuple[dict, str]:
    if not query_id or not dataset_version or plotted_rows < 0:
        raise ValueError("missing chart identity")
    if axis_domain[0] >= axis_domain[1]:
        raise ValueError("invalid axis domain")
    manifest = {
        "query_id": query_id,
        "dataset_version": dataset_version,
        "filters": {key: sorted(set(values))
                    for key, values in sorted(filters.items())},
        "y_axis_domain": list(axis_domain),
        "plotted_rows": plotted_rows,
        "unit": "minutes",
        "render_contract": "depot-delay-v3",
    }
    payload = json.dumps(manifest, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"),
                         ensure_ascii=False).encode("utf-8")
    return manifest, hashlib.sha256(payload).hexdigest()

first = chart_manifest("depot-delay-week", "snapshot-81",
                       {"region": ["north", "north"]}, (0, 47), 31)
second = chart_manifest("depot-delay-week", "snapshot-81",
                        {"region": ["north"]}, (0, 47), 31)
assert first == second and len(first[1]) == 64

Performance and operating cost

For F total filter values and M serialized manifest bytes, sorting normalized filters costs O(F log F) in the worst case; JSON encoding and SHA-256 hashing take O(M) time and O(M) temporary memory. Exporting an image or plotted data can cost much more and depends on the renderer and row count. This hash identifies equal manifest bytes, not equal pixels or trustworthy provenance. Add a data-file checksum and a signed release record when the export package crosses a trust boundary.

Common Mistakes

  • Publishing only a screenshot when reviewers need the plotted data and cohort definition.
  • Exporting a CSV from a stale filter state while the chart shows a newer selection.
  • Assuming a manifest hash proves who created the data.
  • Embedding hidden private rows in an otherwise public SVG or HTML export.

Validation drill

Export one filtered depot-delay chart as SVG and CSV with a manifest. Change only the filter and verify the manifest digest changes, then rebuild the original chart from its saved version and compare counts and axis bounds.
